name: Liability When Agents Interact
title: Liability When Agents Interact
answer: Liability when agents interact concerns who is responsible when autonomous or semi-autonomous AI agents act with other agents, tools, or people and harm results. It covers contract formation, torts, agency law, product liability, and allocation among developers, deployers, users, and third parties. It also covers multi-agent coordination failures, cascading errors, and unclear chains of causation. The topic sits in emerging legal frameworks because existing doctrines were not written for machine-to-machine interaction.

sections.body: Liability when agents interact concerns who is responsible when autonomous or semi-autonomous AI agents act with other agents, tools, or people and harm results. It covers contract formation, torts, agency law, product liability, and allocation among developers, deployers, users, and third parties. It also covers multi-agent coordination failures, cascading errors, and unclear chains of causation. The topic sits in emerging legal frameworks because existing doctrines were not written for machine-to-machine interaction.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: AI agents run on models, orchestration frameworks, APIs, memory stores, identity and permission systems, logging, and payment or messaging rails. In legal analysis, the infrastructure includes audit logs, trace data, model versions, prompts, tool calls, and access controls that establish what an agent did and under whose authority. Liability questions often turn on whether the operator had visibility and control over these components. The technical stack is therefore also an evidentiary stack.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners map the interaction, identify each agent's role, authority, and degree of autonomy, then trace the causal chain from input to harm. They compare the facts to agency, tort, contract, and product liability principles, and they assess contractual allocations such as indemnities, limitations of liability, and insurance. They may use forensic review of logs, model documentation, and deployment records. The work is often comparative and fact-intensive, because multi-agent systems distribute control across several parties.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Key issues include attribution, provenance of data and decisions, disclosure, human oversight, the rights of affected third parties, and the enforceability of terms between parties who did not negotiate directly. Risk allocation may fall on developers, deployers, integrators, or users depending on control, foreseeability, and contractual terms. Provenance records, audit trails, and model cards help establish what happened and who knew what. The site's tracker of 148 active AI lawsuits and 29 AI case law precedents shows that courts are still shaping these boundaries. No single rule governs all agent interactions.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more regulatory guidance, standardized agent identity and logging, and clearer contractual frameworks for autonomous transactions. Courts may adapt agency and product liability doctrines rather than create entirely new categories. Insurance markets and technical standards may become practical allocation mechanisms. With 6947 state AI bills tracked on this site, the compliance surface will remain fragmented. The direction is toward traceable authority and documented handoffs between agents.
